# Evaluating post‑T‑DXd treatment strategies in HER2‑positive metastatic breast cancer

Sophia Zelizer1,4 · Grace B. Gallagher2 · Mithat Gonen2 · Chau Dang1 · Shanu Modi1 · Sarat Chandarlapaty1,3 · Joshua Z. Drago1

Received: 23 May 2025 / Accepted: 8 October 2025 / Published online: 27 November 2025 © The Author(s) 2025

Abstract Purpose  Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) is an antibody drug conjugate (ADC) approved for the treatment of HER2- positive metastatic breast cancer (MBC). Despite its efficacy, eventual resistance and disease progression are common, and no prospective studies exist to guide therapy in T-DXd-resistant HER2-positive MBC. Methods  This retrospective study analyzed patients with HER2-positive MBC who received cancer-directed therapies following treatment with T-DXd at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. Results  Eighty-one eligible patients were identified, who received 199 lines of therapy collectively. Post-T-DXd therapies included other ADCs, chemotherapy, HER2-targeted antibodies, hormone-based therapy, tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), and clinical trials. The median overall survival (OS) after stopping T-DXd treatment was 19 months, with a median progression-free survival (mPFS) of 3.7 months per subsequent treatment line. Chemotherapy was the most common treatment (42% of treatment lines; mPFS 3.4 months). No single therapeutic approach was clearly superior, although subsets of patients appeared to benefit from hormone therapy or TKIs. In a multivariate analysis including treatment type, treatment line, hormone receptor (HR) status, presence of brain metastases, and reason for T-DXd cessation, patients who discontinued T-DXd due to toxicity, rather than disease progression, had significantly better outcomes on subsequent therapy lines (HR 0.35; p < 0.001). Conclusion  Our study indicates that patients emerge from T-DXd treatment with highly refractory disease. These findings highlight the urgent need for optimized treatment strategies and novel therapeutic options for this patient population.

Keywords  Breast Cancer · HER2-positive · Metastatic · T-DXd · Resistance

## Introduction

Antibody drug conjugates (ADCs) are a class of targeted cancer therapies that combine monoclonal antibodies with cytotoxic payloads, designed to deliver targeted chemotherapy more selectively to cancer cells [1]. This approach is

motivated by the hope of limiting toxicity and enhancing therapeutic precision [2]. Since their initial development, ADCs have been developed to treat a variety of cancers [3]. As of 2024, thirteen ADCs have been approved by the FDA, and hundreds are in pre-clinical or clinical development [4]. Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) is a HER2-targeted ADC that has demonstrated clinical activity in HER2- positive and HER2-low metastatic breast cancer (MBC), among other cancer types [5]. T-DXd combines a cleavable linker with a potent topoisomerase I inhibitor payload [6]. Clinical trials have demonstrated its superiority over several pre-existing HER2-targeting therapies, with significantly prolonged progression-free and overall survival in heavily pretreated patients [7]. T-DXd has also been investigated as the first-line treatment for metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer. Interim results from the DESTINY-Breast09 trial showed superior PFS for T-DXd in combination with

pertuzumab compared to taxane/trastuzumab/pertuzumab, suggesting that this regimen may represent a new first-line therapy in this setting [8]. However, resistance to T-DXd inevitably develops in most patients. Proposed mechanisms of resistance in preclinical studies include downregulation of HER2 expression, altered intracellular trafficking, and development of resistance to the payload [9–11]. Further, tumor heterogeneity in HER2 expression appears to contribute to variability in patient response [12]. The optimal approach to managing patients with HER2-positive MBC who exhibit cancer progression on T-DXd therapy remains uncertain, and at this time, no prospective data exist to guide treatment decisions. This retrospective study evaluates clinical outcomes in patients with HER2-positive MBC who received subsequent cancer-directed treatments after T-DXd. By evaluating progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) across different therapeutic categories, we aimed to better define expectations regarding the benefit of available treatment options, predictors of such benefit, and possibly identify promising treatment strategies for managing T-DXd resistant cancers and thus move toward addressing an urgent unmet need in this patient population.

## Methods

We retrospectively examined baseline characteristics, clinical outcomes, and subsequent treatments for patients after they had received T-DXd for HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC) beginning between 2017 and 2023. Eligible patients were identified through institutional records of all patients who had received T-DXd at MSKCC. Individual chart review was performed to confirm eligibility and extract clinical data. We delineated six categories of treatment in the post-T-DXd setting: monoclonal antibodies (mABs), ADC, chemotherapy-based treatment, hormone-based therapy, tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) based therapy, and clinical trials/novel combinations. Descriptive statistics were evaluated at the patient level, and median OS and mPFS were estimated for each patient using the Kaplan–Meier method. Treatment lines were then evaluated individually. The mPFS per treatment line was evaluated, and further stratified by treatment type, using the Kaplan–Meier method. PFS univariate analyses were performed using Cox proportional hazards regression, clustering by patient, looking at treatment type, treatment line, reason for T-DXd cessation, hormone receptor (HR) status, and the presence of brain metastases prior to the event. Hazard ratios and 95% confidence intervals were reported, as well as a global p value for variable significance. Multivariate analyses

were then conducted, adjusting for the variables listed. Progression-free survival was also evaluated per treatment line, stratified by reason for T-DXd cessation. Exploratory analyses were conducted to determine differences in survival time between post-T-DXd HER2 positivity, evaluated using a log-rank test. All analyses were completed in R 4.4.1.

## Results

Demographics

There were 81 patients who met inclusion criteria for this study. The median age at the initiation of T-DXd treatment was 52.0 years. Patients had received a median of four prior lines of therapy before T-DXd (IQR 3.0, 7.0) and underwent a median of two therapies post-T-DXd treatments (IQR 1.0, 3.0). The median duration of T-DXd therapy was 10.1 months (IQR 5.1, 15.4). The reasons for discontinuation of T-DXd included disease progression (78%), pneumonitisrelated toxicity (11%), and other toxicities (11%). Regarding hormone receptor (HR) status, 60% of patients were HR positive, while 40% were HR negative. De novo MBC was present in 37% of patients. Baseline HER2 immunohistochemistry (IHC) revealed that 67% of patients had HER2 3 + tumors, and 33% had HER2 2 + tumors (FISH amplified). Brain metastases were observed in 54% of patients at baseline. At the time of analysis, 48% of patients were alive, while 52% were deceased (Table 1).

Clinical outcomes

We categorized post-T-DXd treatments into six distinct types: ADC, clinical trial/novel combination (the latter including off-label approaches), monoclonal antibody therapy (trastuzumab/pertuzumab alone), chemotherapy (given both with and without trastuzumab), hormone therapy, and TKI-based therapy. The mPFS across treatment types was 3.7 months (Supplementary Table 3). The overall survival time per patient was 19 months (Supplementary Table 3). See Fig. 1 for outcomes by treatment line. To summarize, sixteen (20%) patients received at least one ADC after T-DXd, with a median progression-free survival (mPFS) of 2.4 months. The most frequent ADC regimens included sacituzumab govitecan (n = 4) and T-DM1 (n = 3). We note that sacituzumab govitecan was generally selected for patients whose cancer had converted from HER2 positive to HER2 negative. Experimental therapies through clinical trials were administered to 22 (27%) of patients, yielding an mPFS of 4.2 months per treatment line. Hormone-based therapy (most often given with trastuzumab) was used in 13 (16%) of patients, with an mPFS of 9.1 months per line. TKI-based therapies were received by 42 (52%) of patients,

received monoclonal antibodies alone (such as trastuzumab, or trastuzumab/pertuzumab), with a mPFS of 14 months per line (Fig. 1). Of these patients (n = 7), four had discontinued T-DXd due to toxicity and three due to progression. Chemotherapy (most often given with trastuzumab) was the most commonly administered therapy. Forty-nine (60%) patients received at least one line of chemotherapy after T-DXd, with an mPFS of 3.4 months per treatment line. The most frequent chemotherapy regimens included gemcitabine with trastuzumab (n = 15; mPFS = 4.1 months), vinorelbine with trastuzumab (n = 11; mPFS = 4.6 months), and eribulin with trastuzumab (n = 11, mPFS = 2.4 months) (Supplementary Table 3).

Predictors of therapy benefit

To identify predictors of therapy benefit in patients treated post-T-DXd, multivariate analyses and exploratory subgroup analyses were conducted. In univariate analyses, type of treatment (p = 0.02) and T-DXd cessation reason (p < 0.001) achieved statistical significance. In a multivariate analysis, including treatment type, treatment line, T-DXd cessation reason, hormone receptor status, and brain metastases, T-DXd cessation reason was the only variable that emerged as a significant predictor of survival outcomes, with patients who discontinued T-DXd due to disease progression experiencing worse outcomes compared to those who stopped due to toxicity (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.20–0.53, p < 0.001). ## Discussion

This study describes clinical outcomes of patients with HER2-positive MBC treated with subsequent therapies following treatment with T-DXd. We found that no singletreatment approach was clearly superior, although hormone therapy-based and TKI-based therapies show promise for certain subsets of the patient population. nature of T-DXd-resistant HER2-positive MBC. Notably, we found that patients who discontinued T-DXd due to toxicity had significantly better outcomes than those who stopped due to disease progression. Our results have clinical relevance due to the lack of prospective data to guide clinical decision making after T-DXd treatment failure. The findings align with the 2024 study by Isogai et al., tabulating the clinical course of 29 patients, which also reported the general lack of efficacy and absent consensus on optimal post-T-DXd therapies, highlighting the challenges of managing this heavily pretreated population [13]. Additionally, our study uniquely identifies toxicity-related discontinuation as a significant predictor of improved outcomes, a factor not emphasized in previous analyses. This suggests that cancers which develop clinical resistance to T-DXd may gain biologic cross resistance to other treatments. The mechanism of resistance to T-DXd is unknown; however, some studies have suggested that changes in HER2 expression or surface dynamics may play an important role, and acquisition of more generalized pharmacologic resistance to chemotherapeutics may also contribute [14–16]. Regrettably few patients in this population had paired biopsies to assess; however, despite small numbers, we do note a trend suggesting that loss of HER2 expression may confer resistance to subsequent HER2-targeted therapies. We note that all patients with HER2-loss in our study also stopped T-DXd for disease progression rather than toxicity. We hypothesize that patients who stop T-DXd due progression have higher incidence of HER2-downregulation as a mechanism T-DXd resistance, which may influence responses to subsequent therapies. However, further studies are needed to investigate these questions, as developing rational strategies to treat T-DXdresistant breast cancer remains a pressing clinical need, and a switch in fundamental therapeutic strategy may be required. The retrospective, single-institution nature of this study introduces certain limitations, including restricted generalizability. We note that our study population received T-DXd in later lines than reflected in the current FDA label and also had high prevalence of brain metastases and other high-risk features. These factors, some reflective of realworld populations, may explain the deviation between our results and those reported from clinical trials of T-DXd in HER2-positive MBC [17, 18]. Additionally, the small sample sizes for certain therapy categories limit the statistical power of some of our findings. Another limitation is that this analysis was restricted to patients with HER2- positive disease and did not include those with HER2-low tumors. Despite these constraints, this study highlights the urgent need for further clinical trials to optimize treatment strategies in this population. As T-DXd is now being

incorporated into earlier lines of therapy, additional studies are required to define treatment approaches after progression, including prospective investigations into the sequencing of ADCs [19]. TKI- and hormone-based therapeutic approaches warrant further investigation, as they seem to be highly effective in small patient subsets. The latter option is of particular interest, given the results of the PATINA trial, which highlighted the role that hormone therapy, particularly including a CDK4/6 inhibitor, can play in metastatic HR-positive/HER2-positive breast cancer [20]. In summary, patients with HER2-positive MBC whose cancer progresses on T-DXd face highly refractory disease, with limited progression-free survival across subsequent treatment lines. This study underscores the complexity of treating this patient population and highlights the lack of a clearly superior therapeutic approach in the post-T- DXd setting, where overall prognosis remains poor. These findings emphasize the need for more effective therapies and research into the resistance mechanisms underlying T-DXd failure. Addressing these challenges will require coordinated clinical and translational efforts. Ultimately, advancing understanding of resistance pathways and developing innovative treatment strategies are critical to improving outcomes for this important vulnerable patient population.
